lessons.title: CPU Architecture & the Fetch-Execute Cycle
lessons.description: How registers, the ALU and the control unit run the CPU's fetch-execute cycle.
lessons.content_html:
Inside every computer, from a phone to a games console, sits the central processing unit, or CPU. Its single job is to process instructions: it takes the instructions that make up a program and carries them out, one after another, to make the machine do useful work.

The CPU does this by repeating the same routine over and over, billions of times every second. That routine is called the fetch-execute cycle. To understand how a processor works, you need to know the parts inside it and the steps of this cycle.

The main parts of the CPU

The Arithmetic Logic Unit, usually shortened to ALU, is where the actual calculations happen. It performs arithmetic such as addition and subtraction, and logic operations such as comparing two values to see which is larger or whether they are equal.

The Control Unit, or CU, is the manager of the processor. It decodes each instruction to work out what needs to happen, then sends out control signals that tell the other parts of the computer what to do and when. In this way it coordinates the flow of data around the CPU.

The cache is a small amount of very fast memory built into, or very close to, the CPU. It keeps copies of the data and instructions the processor uses most often, so the CPU can grab them almost instantly instead of waiting for the slower main memory each time.

Finally, the CPU contains a handful of registers. These are tiny storage locations, each able to hold just one value at a time, but they are the fastest storage in the whole computer. The CPU uses them to hold the exact pieces of data and addresses it is working with at that instant.

Key Fact

The ALU does the calculations, the control unit decodes instructions and coordinates the other parts, the cache stores frequently used data for fast access, and registers hold the single values the CPU is using right now.

Von Neumann architecture

Most computers are built using Von Neumann architecture, named after the mathematician John von Neumann. Its key idea is that both the program instructions and the data they work on are stored together in the same memory, and the CPU fetches and carries out those instructions one at a time, in order.

This design relies on a set of special registers. The Program Counter holds the address of the next instruction the CPU will fetch. The Memory Address Register, or MAR, holds the address of the memory location the CPU wants to use next.

The Memory Data Register, or MDR, holds the actual data or instruction that has just been read from memory, or that is about to be written to it. The Accumulator stores the result of the calculations the ALU has just performed.

Key Fact

A register stores either an address or a piece of data. The Program Counter and the MAR store addresses; the MDR and the Accumulator store data. Knowing which each one holds is the key to register questions.

The fetch-execute cycle

Everything the CPU does is built from three repeating stages: fetch, decode and execute. The processor runs through these stages for every single instruction in a program, then loops straight back to the start for the next one.

In the fetch stage, the Program Counter gives the address of the next instruction. The instruction is copied from memory into the CPU, and the Program Counter is then increased by one so that it points to the following instruction, ready for next time.

In the decode stage, the Control Unit examines the instruction and works out exactly what it means and which parts of the computer will be needed to carry it out.

In the execute stage, the instruction is actually carried out. This might mean the ALU performing a calculation and placing the result in the Accumulator, or data being loaded from or saved to memory. The cycle then begins again with the next fetch.

Because instructions and data share the same memory and travel to the CPU along the same route, the processor deals with them in order, one at a time. Working step by step like this keeps the computer predictable and reliable, even though it means a single processor can only ever be part-way through one instruction at any moment.

Key Fact

The fetch-execute cycle has three stages that repeat continuously: fetch the next instruction, decode it, then execute it. The CPU carries out this cycle for every instruction in a program.

Put together, these ideas explain how a processor turns a stored program into action. The components each have a clear role, the registers each hold either an address or a value, and the fetch-execute cycle ties them together into the steady rhythm that drives the whole computer.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on this topic usually ask you to describe the purpose of a component or a register, so learn a one-line role for each of the ALU, control unit, cache, Program Counter, MAR, MDR and Accumulator. A very common mistake is to muddle the MAR and the MDR — remember the MAR handles an address while the MDR handles the data. If you are asked what happens at a stage of the cycle, name the stage and say what the CPU actually does, rather than just listing the parts involved.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The CPU processes instructions by repeating the fetch-execute cycle: fetch, decode and execute.
  • The ALU handles calculations, the control unit decodes and coordinates, the cache speeds up access to frequent data, and registers hold the values in use.
  • In Von Neumann architecture, instructions and data share the same memory, and registers such as the Program Counter, MAR, MDR and Accumulator each store a specific address or piece of data.

lessons.title: CPU Performance
lessons.description: How clock speed, cache size and number of cores decide how fast a CPU works.
lessons.content_html:
Two computers can look almost identical yet one feels far quicker than the other. The difference usually comes down to the CPU and how fast it can work through the fetch-execute cycle. We call this its performance: roughly, how many instructions it can carry out each second. Three characteristics have the biggest effect on how well a CPU performs — its clock speed, the size of its cache, and its number of cores.

Understanding each one, and how they combine, lets you explain why a gaming desktop outperforms a budget laptop, and why upgrading just one part of a system does not always give the speed boost you might expect.

Clock speed

Inside every CPU is a clock that sends out a steady electrical pulse. Each pulse triggers the processor to carry out one step of its work. Clock speed is the number of these pulses, or cycles, per second. It is measured in hertz (Hz). Because modern processors are so fast, clock speed is usually given in gigahertz (GHz), where one gigahertz equals one billion cycles per second. A CPU running at 3.5 GHz completes 3.5 billion cycles every single second.

As a rough guide, more cycles per second means more instructions carried out per second, so a higher clock speed usually gives better performance. Pushing a CPU beyond its factory clock speed is called overclocking; it can raise speed but produces extra heat, which is why fast computers need effective cooling such as fans or heat sinks.

Key Fact

One gigahertz (GHz) means one billion clock cycles per second, so a 3.0 GHz CPU completes three billion cycles every second. Clock speed is measured in hertz.

Cache size

Fetching data from the computer’s main memory (RAM) takes time, and while the CPU waits it cannot do useful work. To cut this delay, the CPU contains a small amount of extremely fast memory called cache. Cache holds copies of the data and instructions the CPU uses most often, right beside the processor where they can be reached almost instantly.

When the CPU finds what it needs in the cache, this is a cache hit. When it does not, and has to fetch from slower RAM instead, this is a cache miss. A larger cache can hold more data, so more requests become cache hits and fewer slow trips to RAM are needed. That is why increasing the cache size improves performance.

Cache is usually split into levels. L1 cache is the smallest and fastest, built right into the core. L2 cache is larger but slightly slower. L3 cache is the largest and slowest of the three, though still far faster than RAM. The CPU checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, and only goes out to RAM if the data is not in any level of cache.

Key Fact

Cache is small, fast memory inside the CPU that stores frequently used data and instructions. A cache hit avoids a slower trip to RAM; a larger cache produces more hits.

Number of cores

A core is a complete processing unit inside the CPU that can run the fetch-execute cycle by itself. Early CPUs had a single core and could only work on one instruction at a time. Modern CPUs are usually multi-core — dual-core (two cores), quad-core (four) or even octa-core (eight) — with several cores built onto one chip.

Having more cores lets a CPU carry out parallel processing: different cores work on different instructions at the same moment. In theory a quad-core CPU can handle four sets of instructions at once, which is a real advantage when running several programs together, or one program written to share its work across cores.

More cores only help if the software is written to split its work into parts that can run at the same time. Some tasks are sequential — each step depends on the result of the last — and cannot be shared out, so they run no faster on eight cores than on one. Cores also share resources such as memory, so doubling the number of cores rarely doubles real-world performance.

How the three work together

These characteristics affect performance both individually and in combination. A CPU with a very high clock speed but a tiny cache may keep stalling while it waits for data from RAM. Adding more cores helps with several tasks at once but does little for a single, simple job that only uses one core. The strongest processors balance all three: a fast clock, a generous cache and several cores.

There are trade-offs, too. Higher clock speeds and extra cores both draw more electrical power and give off more heat, which matters in laptops and phones where battery life and cooling are limited. Designers pick the balance that suits the device, which is why the CPU in a desktop gaming PC is built very differently from the chip in a smartphone.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to explain how a characteristic affects performance, always give the reason as well as the effect — for example, ‘a larger cache stores more data, so there are more cache hits and fewer slow trips to RAM, which speeds the CPU up’. For higher-mark ‘discuss’ questions, weigh up more than one characteristic and remember that extra cores only help software that is written to use them.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Clock speed is how many cycles per second a CPU performs, measured in gigahertz; a higher clock speed usually means more instructions carried out each second.
  • Cache is small, fast memory inside the CPU; a larger cache means more cache hits and fewer slow trips to main memory.
  • More cores allow parallel processing, but only benefit tasks and software that can be split across them.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that each core can run the fetch-execute cycle independently, so several cores allow parallel processing where different instructions run at the same time, increasing the amount of work done per second, and notes this depends on software being able to share the work. practice_questions.text: A student wants to upgrade their computer so that it runs demanding video-editing software much more quickly. Discuss the CPU characteristics they should consider and how each would affect performance.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained discussion of all three characteristics. Clock speed raises the number of cycles per second; a larger cache reduces slow fetches from RAM; more cores enable parallel processing, which suits video editing if the software is multi-threaded. Weighs the characteristics against each other, notes trade-offs such as heat and power, and reaches a justified conclusion about the most useful upgrade. Secure: Discusses at least two characteristics with correct effects and gives a reasoned recommendation. lessons.title: Embedded Systems
lessons.description: What embedded systems are, why everyday devices use them, and how they differ from PCs.
lessons.content_html:
What Is an Embedded System?

An embedded system is a computer built into a larger device to carry out one dedicated function. Unlike a laptop, you do not sit down and type at it — it sits hidden inside a product, quietly controlling how that product works. A washing machine is a good example: a small computer inside it reads the buttons you press, then switches the water, drum motor and heater on and off in the right order to run your chosen wash. That computer only ever runs the washing programme. It cannot browse the web, play games or run a word processor, because it was designed to do one job and do it well.

Key Fact

An embedded system is a computer that is part of a larger device and is designed to perform a single dedicated task, such as controlling a washing machine or a microwave.

What Is Inside an Embedded System?

At the heart of most embedded systems is a microcontroller — a single chip that combines a processor, a small amount of memory and input/output connections in one package. Putting everything on one chip keeps the device small and cheap. The program the microcontroller runs is called firmware, and it is usually stored in read-only memory so that it is ready the moment the device is switched on and is not lost when the power is turned off.

Because the device only has to do one job, designers give it just enough processing power and memory to do that job — no more. A microwave’s controller does not need the power of a desktop PC, so fitting a large, expensive processor would only waste money and energy. This ‘just enough’ approach is one of the main reasons embedded systems are so cheap to make in huge numbers.

On a laptop you install and delete programs all the time — software is meant to change. Firmware is different: it is written once for the device and normally stays the same for the product’s whole life. Some modern products, such as smart TVs and routers, do let their firmware be updated to fix bugs or add features, but for most simple appliances the firmware is fixed and the user never changes it.

Typical Characteristics

Embedded systems share a recognisable set of features. They are dedicated to one task, small enough to fit inside another product, low-powered so they run cool and cheaply, and low-cost because they are produced in huge numbers. They are also built to be reliable: a pacemaker or a car braking system must work perfectly every time, so the hardware and firmware are kept simple and thoroughly tested.

Many embedded systems are also real-time systems, meaning they must respond to inputs straight away rather than after a delay. When a car’s anti-lock braking system senses a wheel starting to lock, it has to react in a fraction of a second — a late response would be useless. Reacting instantly and predictably is often more important for these systems than raw processing speed.

Key Fact

Typical embedded systems are dedicated to one function, small, low-cost, low-power and highly reliable — and many must respond in real time.

Using an embedded system instead of fitting a full computer brings clear benefits. Because the hardware only does one job, it can be made smaller, cheaper and more energy-efficient, and there is less that can go wrong, so it is more reliable. The trade-off is flexibility: an embedded system cannot easily be upgraded or given new tasks, and if the firmware has a fault it can be hard to fix once the product has been sold.

Examples of Embedded Systems

Embedded systems are all around you, usually without you noticing. In the home they control washing machines, dishwashers, microwaves and central-heating thermostats. In transport they run the engine-management and anti-lock braking systems in cars, and the controllers inside traffic lights. In healthcare they power devices such as pacemakers. In leisure and personal technology they appear in digital cameras, fitness trackers and MP3 players. In every case the same idea applies: a computer is built into the product to control one specific set of tasks.

Embedded vs General-Purpose Computers

A general-purpose computer, such as a desktop PC, laptop, tablet or smartphone, is designed to run many different programs. You can install new software, delete it, and use the same machine for writing, gaming, video calls and browsing. It has a full operating system, plenty of memory and storage, and is built to be upgraded over time.

An embedded system is the opposite. Its function is fixed when it is manufactured, its firmware is not meant to be changed by the user, and it usually has only the memory and processing power its single task requires. In short, a general-purpose computer is a flexible machine you adapt to many jobs, while an embedded system is a specialised machine dedicated to just one.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Watch your command words. If a question says ‘state’ or ‘give’, a short phrase is enough; if it says ‘describe’ or ‘explain’, you must add why or how. A common mistake is naming a laptop, tablet or smartphone as an example of an embedded system — these are general-purpose computers, so always pick a device that does one fixed job, such as a microwave or a traffic-light controller. For the longer discuss question, cover both types of computer and back up your points with clear examples.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An embedded system is a computer built into a larger device to perform one dedicated task, usually based around a microcontroller running fixed firmware.
  • Typical embedded systems are dedicated, small, low-cost, low-power and reliable, and many are real-time systems that must respond immediately.
  • A general-purpose computer runs many different, upgradeable programs, while an embedded system does one fixed job it was designed and manufactured for.

lessons.title: Primary Storage (RAM, ROM & Virtual Memory)
lessons.description: How RAM, ROM and virtual memory work together to keep a computer running.
lessons.content_html:
Every time you open an app, load a game or start typing an essay, the processor needs somewhere to keep the instructions and data it is working on at that exact moment. That job belongs to primary storage, which is usually just called memory. It sits between the CPU and the much slower secondary storage, such as a hard drive or solid state drive.

The CPU can only work with data that is held in primary storage, because that is the only storage it is able to read from directly. Anything saved on secondary storage has to be copied into memory first before the processor can touch it. This is the whole reason computers need memory: without it, the CPU would have nothing to fetch and execute.

In a typical computer, primary storage is made up of two main types of memory: RAM and ROM. They sound similar and both sit close to the processor, but they do very different jobs, and exam questions love to test whether you can tell them apart.

RAM — the computer’s working memory

RAM stands for Random Access Memory. It holds the operating system, the applications you currently have open and the files you are actively using. When you launch a program, a copy of it is loaded from secondary storage into RAM so that the CPU can reach it quickly. The more RAM a computer has, the more programs it can keep running smoothly at the same time.

RAM has two defining characteristics. First, it can be both read from and written to, so its contents change constantly as you use the machine. Second, it is volatile, which means everything stored in it is lost the instant the power is turned off. That is why unsaved work vanishes if your computer suddenly shuts down.

A useful way to picture this is a desk. RAM is like the top of the desk, where you spread out the books and papers you are using right now so you can reach them quickly. Secondary storage is like the filing cabinet in the corner: it holds far more, but you have to get up and fetch things from it before you can work on them. A bigger desk lets you have more open at once, just as more RAM lets you run more programs.

Key Fact

RAM is volatile and can be both read from and written to. It stores the programs, data and operating system that are in use right now, and loses everything when the power is cut.

ROM — the start-up memory

ROM stands for Read Only Memory. As the name suggests, under normal use it can only be read from, not written to, so its contents stay fixed. ROM is non-volatile, which means it holds on to its data even when the computer is switched off.

The main purpose of ROM is to store the small set of start-up instructions the computer needs the instant it is switched on. This program is often called the bootstrap. It tells the computer how to check its hardware and then load the operating system from secondary storage into RAM so the machine can begin working.

When the power button is pressed, RAM is empty, so the CPU has nothing to run. It turns to ROM, which is non-volatile and still holds the bootstrap instructions. The CPU follows these instructions to test the hardware and then copy the operating system from secondary storage into RAM. Once the operating system is loaded, the computer is ready to use. Keeping these instructions in ROM guarantees they are always there, even after the machine has been unplugged for weeks.

Telling RAM and ROM apart

The clearest way to compare the two is by three features: whether they are volatile, whether they can be written to, and what they store. RAM is volatile, can be read and written, and holds whatever is running now. ROM is non-volatile, is normally read only, and holds the fixed start-up instructions. RAM is also usually much larger than ROM, because it has to hold everything currently in use, whereas ROM only needs room for a small boot program.

Key Fact

ROM is non-volatile and read only, and stores the boot-up (bootstrap) instructions. RAM is volatile and read-write, and stores the programs and data in current use.

Virtual memory

RAM is fast but limited in size. If you open too many programs, or a single program is very large, RAM can fill up completely. When that happens, the computer uses a technique called virtual memory. A section of the secondary storage — the hard drive or solid state drive — is set aside and treated as though it were extra RAM.

Here is how it works. Data in RAM that is not being used at that moment is moved out of RAM and written to this reserved area of secondary storage. That frees up space in RAM for the programs the user is actively working with. When the moved data is needed again, it is copied back into RAM, and other unused data may be swapped out to make room. This constant transfer of data between RAM and secondary storage is what keeps a full system running instead of freezing.

Secondary storage is far slower to read and write than RAM. Every time data is swapped between RAM and virtual memory, the CPU has to wait for the slow secondary storage to catch up. If RAM is very full, the computer can end up spending more time shuffling data back and forth than doing useful work, and everything feels sluggish. Fitting more RAM is the best fix, because the computer then rarely needs to fall back on virtual memory at all.

Key Fact

When RAM is full, the computer moves data that is not currently in use out to a reserved area of secondary storage called virtual memory, then swaps it back into RAM when it is needed again.

So the three types of memory work as a team. ROM gets the machine started, RAM gives the processor a fast place to work, and virtual memory acts as a safety net when RAM runs out. Understanding which is volatile, which can be written to, and what each one stores is the key to answering almost any question on primary storage.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A very common mistake is to describe ROM simply as memory that can never be changed. Instead, say that it is read only under normal use and that it stores the start-up (bootstrap) instructions. When a question asks you to explain the difference between RAM and ROM, do not just list features — make clear comparison points about volatility, whether each can be written to, and what each one stores. If a question is about a slow computer, link full RAM to the use of virtual memory and remember that adding more RAM is the strongest improvement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • RAM is volatile, read-write memory that holds the operating system, programs and data in current use; ROM is non-volatile, read-only memory that holds the start-up instructions.
  • The CPU can only work with data held in primary storage, so programs must be copied from secondary storage into RAM before they can run.
  • When RAM is full, virtual memory uses a slower area of secondary storage as extra RAM, which keeps the system running but reduces performance.

lessons.title: Secondary Storage
lessons.description: How magnetic, optical and solid-state storage work and when to use each type.
lessons.content_html:
Why Computers Need Secondary Storage

When you switch a computer off, the working memory it was using empties completely. That memory is volatile, which means it only holds data while power is flowing. If a computer had nothing else, every file, photo and program would vanish the moment you unplugged it. This is why every computer also has secondary storage — storage that is non-volatile, so it keeps its contents safely even with the power off.

Secondary storage does two big jobs. First, it stores everything permanently: the operating system, your applications, and all your saved documents, music and pictures. Second, it gives a computer a huge amount of room. Working memory is fast but small and expensive, so it is measured in a few gigabytes. Secondary storage is much larger and far cheaper for each gigabyte, which is why a laptop can hold thousands of files while only running a handful of them at once.

Key Fact

Secondary storage is non-volatile: it keeps its data without power. That is exactly why it is used to store the operating system, programs and files permanently — unlike volatile working memory, which loses everything when the power is removed.

Three Families of Secondary Storage

There are three main types of secondary storage, and each one records data in a completely different way. Magnetic storage uses magnetism on spinning surfaces, optical storage uses a laser and a shiny disc, and solid-state storage uses electronic memory chips with no moving parts. Because they work differently, each type is good at some things and weak at others, so choosing the right one depends on the job.

Magnetic Storage

Magnetic storage is the technology inside a traditional hard disk drive (HDD). Data is stored as tiny magnetised patterns on the surface of fast-spinning metal platters. A read/write head floats just above each platter and moves across it to reach the right spot; it detects the magnetism to read data, or changes it to write new data. Every magnetised area represents a binary 1 or 0.

Because the platters spin and the head moves, magnetic drives have moving parts. This makes them slower than solid-state storage and easier to damage if the computer is dropped or knocked. Their great strength is capacity for the price: a single hard disk drive can hold several terabytes and costs very little per gigabyte, which is why they are still common in desktop computers and servers that need to store a lot cheaply.

A second form of magnetic storage is magnetic tape. Tape holds an enormous amount of data at a very low cost, but it is sequential: to reach a particular file the drive must wind through the tape in order, rather than jumping straight to it. That makes tape too slow for everyday use, but ideal for backing up and archiving large amounts of data that are rarely read back.

Optical Storage

Optical storage covers CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs. Data is stored along a spiral track as microscopic pits and lands — tiny bumps and flat areas on the disc’s reflective surface. A laser shines onto the track, and the way the light reflects back tells the drive whether it is reading a 1 or a 0.

Optical discs are cheap to produce and easy to carry, so they were widely used to hand out films, music and software. Their weakness is capacity: a CD holds only about 700 megabytes, a single-layer DVD about 4.7 gigabytes, and a single-layer Blu-ray disc about 25 gigabytes. Discs are also fairly slow to read and are easily scratched, which can make the data unreadable.

Key Fact

The optical capacity ladder rises steadily: a CD holds roughly 700 MB, a single-layer DVD about 4.7 GB, and a single-layer Blu-ray disc around 25 GB. Newer formats pack more data into the same size of disc.

Solid-State Storage

Solid-state storage stores data electronically inside flash memory chips. It has no moving parts at all — there is nothing to spin and no head to move. This technology is found in solid-state drives (SSDs), USB flash drives and the memory cards used in cameras and phones.

Having no moving parts brings real advantages. Solid-state storage is the fastest type of secondary storage, it is much more durable because it can survive knocks and drops, and it is silent and uses little power. Those qualities make it perfect for laptops, phones and portable drives. The trade-offs are that it costs more per gigabyte than a magnetic drive, and each memory cell can only be rewritten a limited number of times before it wears out.

Key Fact

An SSD has no moving parts, so it is both faster and more durable than a magnetic hard disk drive. Its main drawbacks are a higher cost per gigabyte and a limited number of times each cell can be rewritten.

Weighing Up the Trade-offs

No type of storage wins on everything, so devices are compared on six characteristics: capacity (how much it holds), speed (how quickly data is read or written), portability (how easy it is to carry), durability (how well it survives damage), reliability (how likely it is to keep working without losing data), and cost (usually measured per gigabyte). The best choice is always a balance of these.

The table below sums up how the three families compare across the main characteristics.

CharacteristicMagnetic (HDD/tape)Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray)Solid-state (SSD/flash)
CapacityVery high (terabytes)Low (700 MB – 25 GB)High, but pricier
SpeedMediumSlowFastest
PortabilityTape and discs portable; internal drives less soVery portableVery portable
DurabilityLow — moving partsLow — scratches easilyHigh — no moving parts
Cost per GBCheapestCheap per discMost expensive

Reliability is worth a closer look. A magnetic drive can fail suddenly if its moving parts break, especially after a knock. Optical discs degrade over time and stop working once scratched. Solid-state storage has no parts to break, so it is generally very reliable, but remember that its cells wear out after a great many writes — so no single type is perfectly dependable, and important data should always be backed up.

An everyday laptop: a solid-state drive is the best fit. It is fast, it survives being carried around, it is silent and it saves battery — speed and durability matter more here than the extra cost.

Backing up a large amount of data cheaply: magnetic tape or a high-capacity hard disk drive wins. Both offer enormous capacity for a very low cost per gigabyte, and slow access does not matter for backups that are rarely read.

Handing out a film or software to many people: an optical disc is ideal. Discs are cheap to produce in bulk and easy to post or carry, and the small capacity is enough for the files.

Moving files between two computers: a USB flash drive — a small solid-state device — is convenient, portable and quick for the modest amounts of data involved.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Read the command word carefully. State or identify questions only want a short fact, such as naming a device or a capacity, so do not waste time explaining. Describe asks how something works, while compare means you must contrast two types against the same characteristic in one sentence — for example, “an SSD is faster than an HDD because it has no moving parts to wait for.” A common mistake is listing features of each device separately instead of linking them. When a question gives a scenario, always name a specific device and then justify it using the characteristics that matter most for that situation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Secondary storage is non-volatile, so it keeps the operating system, programs and files permanently — and offers far more room at a lower cost per gigabyte than working memory.
  • The three types work differently: magnetic uses magnetised patterns on spinning platters, optical uses a laser on pits and lands, and solid-state uses flash memory chips with no moving parts.
  • Compare devices on capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability and cost: SSDs are fastest and most durable, magnetic storage is cheapest for bulk data, and optical discs are cheap and portable but low-capacity.

lessons.title: Data Representation (Binary, Hex & Character Sets)
lessons.description: Number bases, binary addition and shifts, and how ASCII and Unicode store text as binary.
lessons.content_html:
Why Computers Work in Binary

Deep inside every computer are billions of tiny electronic switches. Each switch can only ever be in one of two states: on or off. Because of this, a computer stores and processes everything — numbers, text, images and sound — using just two digits, 0 and 1. This two-digit system is called binary, or base 2. The numbers you use every day are made from the digits 0 to 9 and belong to a different system called denary, or base 10. To be useful, a computer must be able to move smoothly between the two.

Key Fact

A single binary digit, called a bit, can be 0 or 1. Group eight bits together and you can make 256 different patterns, from 00000000 up to 11111111, which represent the denary values 0 to 255.

Reading and Writing Binary Numbers

An 8-bit binary number has eight columns, and each column has a place value that doubles as you move left: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128. The far-left column, worth 128, is the most significant bit, because it makes the biggest difference to the value. The far-right column, worth 1, is the least significant bit. To find the denary value of a binary number, you simply add up the place values wherever there is a 1.

Converting the other way, from denary to binary, works by subtraction. Take the denary number 156. The largest place value that fits is 128, so write a 1 in that column and subtract, leaving 28. Next, 64 and 32 are both too big, so write 0 for each. Then 16 fits into 28, leaving 12; 8 fits, leaving 4; 4 fits, leaving 0; and 2 and 1 are not needed. Reading the columns gives 10011100.

Suppose you are given 10011100 and asked for its denary value. Write the place values above the digits: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Wherever there is a 1, add that place value. Here the 1s sit under 128, 16, 8 and 4, so the total is 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 156. Adding the columns that hold a 1 is all there is to it.

Units of Data

The smallest unit of data is a single bit, one 0 or 1. Four bits together make a nibble, and eight bits make a byte. A byte matters because it is just enough to store one character of text. Larger amounts of storage are measured by multiplying up in steps of one thousand.

A kilobyte (KB) is 1,000 bytes, a megabyte (MB) is 1,000 kilobytes, a gigabyte (GB) is 1,000 megabytes, a terabyte (TB) is 1,000 gigabytes, and a petabyte (PB) is 1,000 terabytes. Each step up multiplies the amount of storage by a thousand, so a one terabyte hard drive holds roughly a trillion bytes of data.

Key Fact

The units of data storage, from smallest to largest, are: bit, nibble, byte, kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte and petabyte. Some devices use 1,024 rather than 1,000 for each step, and either figure is accepted.

Adding Binary Numbers

Computers add binary using four simple rules: 0 + 0 = 0; 0 + 1 = 1; 1 + 1 = 0, carry 1; and 1 + 1 + 1 = 1, carry 1. You work from right to left and carry into the next column, exactly as you do when adding in denary. A problem appears when the answer needs more columns than are available. If two 8-bit numbers add up to more than 255, the result will not fit in 8 bits and the extra carry is lost. This is called an overflow error.

Add 00110101, which is 53, to 00010110, which is 22. Working from the right, a carry is created each time two 1s meet, and the final answer is 01001011. Checking in denary, 53 + 22 = 75, and 01001011 really is 64 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 75.

Now try 11111111 + 00000001. In denary this is 255 + 1 = 256. The answer 100000000 needs nine bits, but only eight are available, so the leading 1 is lost and the byte wrongly reads 00000000. The computer has run out of room, and this overflow makes the stored result incorrect.

Binary Shifts

A binary shift moves every bit a set number of places to the left or right, filling the empty columns with 0s. A shift to the left multiplies the number by two for each place moved, while a shift to the right divides it by two for each place. For example, shifting 00010100, which is 20, two places to the left gives 01010000. Each place doubled the value, so 20 became 20 × 4 = 80, and 01010000 is 64 + 16 = 80. Shift too far and 1s are pushed off the end, where they are lost, which changes the answer.

Hexadecimal

Long strings of 0s and 1s are hard for people to read without slipping up, so programmers often use hexadecimal, or base 16, as a shorthand. Hexadecimal uses sixteen digit symbols: 0 to 9 as normal, then A, B, C, D, E and F standing for the values 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. It is popular because it is compact and it lines up neatly with binary.

The link is simple: one hexadecimal digit represents exactly one nibble of 4 bits, so a whole byte becomes just two hexadecimal digits. To convert, split a byte into two nibbles and turn each into its hex digit. The byte 10011100 splits into 1001 and 1100, which are 9 and 12, or 9 and C, giving the hexadecimal value 9C. Hexadecimal is widely used for the colour codes on web pages and for memory addresses.

Storing Text: Character Sets

Computers store text by giving every letter, digit and symbol its own binary code. The full list of characters a computer can use, together with their codes, is called a character set. The codes are ordered logically, so the letters follow one another in sequence: if the code for ‘A’ is 65, then ‘B’ is 66 and ‘C’ is 67. This tidy ordering makes it easy to sort text alphabetically and to switch between upper and lower case.

The oldest common character set is ASCII, which uses 7 bits per character and can therefore represent 128 different characters — enough for English letters, digits, punctuation and some control codes. That is not nearly enough for every writing system, so Unicode was created. Unicode uses more bits per character, commonly 16 or 32, letting it represent well over a million characters, including alphabets from around the world and emoji. The rule behind both is the same: a set with n bits per character can represent \(2^n\) different characters, so more bits mean more characters but larger files.

Key Fact

The number of characters a set can hold is found with \(2^n\), where n is the number of bits per character. So 7-bit ASCII holds \(2^7 = 128\) characters and 8 bits hold \(2^8 = 256\). A 200-character message stored in 8-bit codes therefore needs 200 × 8 = 1,600 bits, or 200 bytes.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Command words matter here. ‘Convert’ wants you to show your working, not just an answer, so line up your place values or nibbles clearly and let the marker follow your method. ‘Explain’ an overflow error means saying both what it is and why it happens — a result too big for the bits available. A very common slip is muddling the direction of a binary shift: left multiplies, right divides. Always check that your final binary answer has the right number of bits, padding with leading 0s where needed.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Computers store all data in binary because their circuits have only two states; denary and hexadecimal are convenient ways for people to read and write those binary values.
  • Binary can be added, producing carries and sometimes an overflow error, and shifted left or right to multiply or divide by powers of two.
  • Text is stored using a character set: ASCII uses 7 bits for 128 characters, while Unicode uses more bits to cover over a million characters from every language.

lessons.title: Representing Images & Sound
lessons.description: How images are stored as pixels and sound as samples, and why quality drives up file size.
lessons.content_html:
How Computers Store Pictures

A computer can only hold data as binary — long strings of 0s and 1s — so a photograph must be turned into numbers before it can be saved. The most common way to do this is with a bitmap image, which is simply a grid of tiny coloured squares. Each square is a pixel (short for ‘picture element’), the smallest element of a digital image. Every pixel is given a binary code that stands for its colour, so the whole picture becomes a long list of colour codes that the computer reads row by row to rebuild the image.

Key Fact

Colour depth is the number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel. With a colour depth of \(n\) bits, an image can use \(2^n\) different colours — every extra bit doubles the number of colours available.

Colour Depth

The colour depth of an image is the number of bits used to represent the colour of a single pixel. Because each extra bit doubles the patterns available, an image with a colour depth of \(n\) bits can display \(2^n\) colours. A colour depth of just 1 bit gives only \(2^1 = 2\) colours, which are usually black and white.

Raising the colour depth quickly widens the range of colours. An 8-bit colour depth stores \(2^8 = 256\) colours, while 24-bit colour — often called ‘true colour’ — stores \(2^{24}\), which is over 16 million shades. That is more than the human eye can easily tell apart, so it produces smooth, realistic images. The catch is that more bits per pixel means every pixel takes up more storage.

Resolution

The resolution of a bitmap image is the number of pixels it contains, usually written as width times height, such as 1920 by 1080. A higher resolution packs in more pixels, so the image holds more detail and looks sharper. A low-resolution image stretched across a large screen looks blocky, because each pixel is enlarged until you can see the individual squares.

Colour depth and resolution each affect two things at once: the quality of the picture and the size of its file. Turning either one up makes the image look better but also makes the file bigger, because there is simply more information to record. Balancing that trade-off is a choice designers make every time they save an image.

Key Fact

Increasing the colour depth or the resolution improves image quality but increases the file size, because each change adds more binary data that has to be stored.

The size of a bitmap image in bits is found by multiplying the colour depth by the number of pixels:

$$\text{file size (bits)} = \text{colour depth} \times \text{width} \times \text{height}$$

For example, take an image that is 200 pixels wide and 300 pixels high with a colour depth of 8 bits. Its size is \(8 \times 200 \times 300\), which comes to 480,000 bits. To change bits into bytes you divide by 8, giving 60,000 bytes, or roughly 60 kilobytes. Notice that doubling either the colour depth or the resolution would double the file size.

Metadata

When an image is saved, the file also stores metadata, which means ‘data about the data’. Metadata is the extra information the computer needs in order to open and display the picture correctly, such as the image’s width, height and colour depth. It often records other details too, like the date the photo was taken and the camera settings, and many phones add the location where it was captured. Without the width and height, the computer would not know the shape of the pixel grid, so it could not rebuild the image at all.

Key Fact

Metadata is data stored alongside an image that describes it — for example its width, height and colour depth. The computer relies on this information to reconstruct and display the image correctly.

How Computers Store Sound

Sound in the real world is analogue: it is a continuous wave that changes smoothly and can take any value. A computer cannot store a continuous wave, because it works only in binary, so the sound must first be converted into numbers. This is done by sampling — measuring the height, or amplitude, of the wave at regular moments and recording each measurement as a binary number.

Two settings control how faithfully the wave is captured. The sample rate is how many samples are taken every second, measured in Hertz (Hz). Music on a CD, for instance, uses a sample rate of 44,100 Hz, meaning the wave is measured 44,100 times a second. Taking more samples each second captures quicker changes in the sound, so the recording stays closer to the original.

The bit depth is the number of bits used to store each individual sample, such as 16 bits. A larger bit depth lets each sample record the amplitude more precisely, giving a wider range of volumes and a cleaner sound. The duration is simply how many seconds of audio the file contains; a longer recording needs more samples and therefore more storage.

Key Fact

A higher sample rate and a greater bit depth both make a digital recording sound closer to the original, but both also increase the size of the sound file.

Quality versus File Size

Just like images, sound files involve a trade-off between quality and size. Raising the sample rate, raising the bit depth, or recording for longer all improve or lengthen the audio, yet each one increases the number of bits that must be stored. That is why a short, low-quality voice memo takes up far less space than a long, high-quality music track.

The size of a sound file in bits is found by multiplying its three settings together:

$$\text{file size (bits)} = \text{sample rate} \times \text{duration (s)} \times \text{bit depth}$$

For example, a 30-second clip recorded at a sample rate of 44,100 Hz with a bit depth of 16 bits has a size of \(44100 \times 30 \times 16\), which comes to 21,168,000 bits. Dividing by 8 gives 2,646,000 bytes, or about 2.6 megabytes.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions, always show your working: state the formula, substitute the numbers, then give the answer with its unit — method marks are still available even if the final figure is wrong. Answers come out in bits, so if a question asks for bytes, remember to divide by 8. When you are asked to describe or explain the effect of colour depth, resolution, sample rate or bit depth, name both consequences — the change in quality and the change in file size — because a one-sided answer will not earn full marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bitmap images are grids of pixels: colour depth sets the bits per pixel (giving 2 to the power of the depth colours) and resolution sets the number of pixels.
  • Sound is stored by sampling an analogue wave, with sample rate (in Hertz), bit depth and duration deciding how accurate the recording is.
  • Turning up colour depth, resolution, sample rate or bit depth improves quality but always increases the file size.

lessons.title: Data Compression
lessons.description: Why files are compressed and how lossless and lossy compression differ in what they keep.
lessons.content_html:
Why We Compress Files

Modern files can be enormous. A single high-quality photo, song or video can take up millions of bytes, and moving all of that data across a network takes time and uses up capacity. Compression is the answer: it shrinks a file so it uses less storage space and travels faster. Compressed files download and upload more quickly, they use less bandwidth, web pages containing them load sooner, and more of them fit inside an email attachment limit or a backup drive. In short, compression saves both space and time.

Key Fact

Files are compressed to save storage space and to move them faster over a network. Everyday examples include streaming music and video, sending email attachments, loading images on a web page, and backing up large amounts of data.

Two Families: Lossless and Lossy

There are two main approaches to compression, and the difference between them comes down to a single question: is any of the original data thrown away? A lossless method keeps every bit; a lossy method deletes some data for good. Choosing between them is one of the most important decisions when storing or sending a file.

Lossless Compression

Lossless compression makes a file smaller without losing any information at all. It works by spotting redundancy — data that is repeated or predictable — and recording it in a more efficient way. A matching program can then reverse the process and reconstruct the original file perfectly. Because nothing is thrown away, lossless compression is essential wherever every character matters, such as text documents, spreadsheets and program files. Familiar lossless formats include ZIP archives, PNG images and FLAC audio.

The trade-off is that lossless compression usually cannot shrink a file as much as lossy compression can, because it is only allowed to reorganise data, never to remove it. What you gain is certainty: the restored file is identical to the one you started with.

One simple lossless method is run-length encoding. Instead of listing a run of the same value over and over, it stores the value once together with a count of how many times it repeats. A line of forty identical white pixels can be recorded as ‘white, 40’ rather than writing ‘white’ forty times. This works brilliantly on images with large blocks of a single colour, but poorly on detailed photographs where colours rarely repeat.

Another method is Huffman coding, which gives the most common characters the shortest binary codes and the rarer ones longer codes, so the whole file needs fewer bits overall. Both methods are fully reversible, and that reversibility is exactly what makes them lossless.

Key Fact

Lossless compression loses no data. The original file can be rebuilt perfectly, bit for bit, which is why it is used for text, spreadsheets and program code where a single wrong character could ruin the file.

Lossy Compression

Lossy compression takes a bolder approach: it permanently removes some of the data to make the file far smaller. The detail it discards is chosen carefully — usually parts that humans are unlikely to notice. The catch is that once this data is gone, it is gone for good, so the original file can never be recovered exactly.

Lossy compression is ideal for photos, music and video, where a small drop in quality is a fair price for a huge saving in size. JPEG images and MP3 audio are the best-known examples. An MP3, for instance, removes sounds that are hard for the human ear to pick out, such as very quiet notes that are drowned out by louder ones, shrinking a song to a small fraction of the size of the uncompressed original.

With lossy compression you choose a balance between file size and quality. Compress a little and the loss is almost invisible; compress heavily and pictures turn blocky or blurry and audio sounds muddy. The right amount depends on how the file will be used.

Because the process is not reversible, editing a lossy file and re-saving it as lossy again removes even more detail, so quality gets steadily worse with each save. This is why photographers and musicians keep a lossless or uncompressed master copy and only export a lossy version at the very end.

Choosing the Right Type

The safest way to decide is to ask whether losing any data would matter. For a legal document, a spreadsheet of exam marks or a program’s code, you must use lossless compression, because a single changed value could corrupt the whole file. For photographs on a website, music streaming or a video call, lossy compression is usually the better choice: the enormous size saving matters more than perfect detail, and the loss is hard to notice anyway.

Key Fact

Lossy compression makes a much smaller file but permanently loses some detail, so the original cannot be recovered. Lossless compression saves less space but keeps every bit, so the original can always be restored exactly.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common trap is thinking that ‘lossless’ means a file has not been compressed — it has been, just without throwing any data away. If a question asks you to compare the two types, make two linked points, for example that lossy gives a much smaller file but permanently loses detail, whereas lossless saves less space but keeps every bit. When you are given a scenario, always justify your choice by asking whether losing data would actually matter for that particular file.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Compression shrinks files so they use less storage and transfer faster — vital for streaming, email attachments and web pages.
  • Lossless compression removes no data and can be reversed perfectly, so it suits text, spreadsheets and program files.
  • Lossy compression permanently deletes detail for a much bigger size saving, so it suits photos, music and video where the loss is hard to notice.

lessons.title: Networks, Topologies & Protocols
lessons.description: How networks are built and shaped, and the rules and addresses that move data between them.
lessons.content_html:
A network is two or more computers or devices connected together so that they can share data and resources such as files, printers and a single internet connection. Almost everything you do online depends on networks, so it helps to understand how they are built and the rules that let different devices work together.

Networks are grouped by the area they cover. A Local Area Network (LAN) covers a small area on a single site, such as a school, home or office, and the organisation that runs it usually owns all of the hardware and cabling. A Wide Area Network (WAN) covers a large area and joins together LANs that may be in different towns, countries or even continents. Because a WAN stretches over such distances, its infrastructure is often leased from telecommunications companies rather than owned outright. The internet is the largest WAN of all.

Key Fact

A LAN covers a small area on one site and is owned by the organisation that runs it; a WAN covers a large area, connects LANs together, and usually relies on leased infrastructure. The internet is the largest WAN.

The speed a network feels to its users depends on several factors. The most important is bandwidth, which is the maximum amount of data a connection can carry in a given time. The more devices that are connected at once, the more they must share that bandwidth, so each device can slow down. Performance is also affected by whether a connection is wired or wireless, the quality of the cabling, and the amount of interference.

Computers can take different roles on a network. In a client-server network, one or more powerful central computers called servers provide services, while the other computers, the clients, request them. This makes security, updates and backups easy to manage from one place, but the server is expensive and, if it fails, every client loses access. In a peer-to-peer network the computers are all equal and each can act as both client and server, sharing files directly. This is cheaper and simpler for a small home network, but it is harder to back up and secure, and it slows down as more peers are added.

Turning stand-alone computers into a working LAN needs several pieces of hardware, each with its own job:

  • A Network Interface Controller (NIC) lets a single device connect to a network and gives it its MAC address.
  • A switch connects devices together inside one LAN and uses their MAC addresses to send data only to the device it is meant for.
  • A router connects different networks together, such as joining a home LAN to the internet, and directs data between them using IP addresses.
  • A wireless access point lets wireless devices join a wired network over Wi-Fi.
  • The transmission media are the cables or signals that actually carry the data, such as copper cable, fibre-optic cable or radio waves.

The internet is a worldwide collection of computer networks — a network of networks — all connected together. To find the computer that stores a particular website, your device uses the Domain Name System (DNS), which is made up of many separate domain name servers. When you type a web address, the DNS looks up the matching IP address so your browser knows which server to connect to. If the first server does not hold that record, the request is simply passed on to another.

Key Fact

The DNS turns a human-friendly web address into the IP address of the server that hosts the website, so your browser can connect to it.

Websites and files are kept available through hosting, where a company stores them on a server that stays connected to the internet all day, every day; a web server then sends those pages to any client that requests them. Many services are now delivered through cloud computing, which means storage, software and processing are provided remotely over the internet instead of running on your own machine.

The cloud lets people work from anywhere, avoids the cost of maintaining local hardware, and can back data up automatically. Its drawbacks are that it depends on a reliable internet connection, charges an ongoing subscription, and raises concerns about the security of data held by someone else.

The topology of a network describes the shape in which its devices are arranged. In a star topology every device has its own cable to a central switch. In a mesh topology devices are connected to many others so that data can travel by more than one route.

A star topology gives each device a dedicated connection, so there are few collisions and performance is good, and if one cable fails only that single device is cut off. Its weakness is that the whole network depends on the central switch: if the switch fails, everything stops, and the design needs a lot of cabling.

A mesh topology has no single point of failure, because if one link breaks the data simply takes another route, which makes it very reliable and good at handling heavy traffic. The drawback is that a fully wired mesh needs a huge amount of cabling and is expensive and complex to set up, which is why mesh networks are often built wirelessly.

Devices connect either by a wired link, usually an Ethernet cable, or wirelessly through Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. A wired connection is faster, more stable and more secure, because an intruder needs physical access to the cable, but it ties devices down and costs more to install. A wireless connection is convenient and lets devices move around freely, but it is usually slower, can suffer interference and dropouts, and is easier to intercept. Bluetooth is a short-range wireless link used to connect personal devices such as headphones or a keyboard.

Because data can be intercepted as it crosses a network, it is often protected by encryption, which scrambles the data using a key so that anyone who intercepts it sees only meaningless characters; only the intended recipient, who holds the key, can turn it back into the original message.

Every device also needs an address so that data reaches the right place. An IP address identifies a device on a network and is used to route data between networks. Older IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long and are written as four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, such as 192.168.0.1; because the world is running out of these, newer IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long and are written as groups of hexadecimal digits. A MAC address, by contrast, is a permanent number built into a device’s network card by its manufacturer, written as twelve hexadecimal digits, and is used to identify a device within a local network.

For devices made by different companies to work together, everyone must follow the same agreed rules, called standards. Without standards, equipment made by one company might not work with equipment made by another. Familiar examples include the agreed character set used to store text and the language used to build web pages.

A protocol is a set of rules that controls how data is transferred between devices, covering things like the format of the data and the order in which messages are sent. Because different jobs need different rules, there are several protocols, each with its own purpose.

Each of these protocols has a specific job:

  • TCP/IP is the core set of rules for the internet: it breaks data into packets, addresses them, routes them across networks and reassembles them at the far end.
  • HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is used to transfer web pages between a web server and a browser.
  • HTTPS is the secure version of HTTP, which encrypts the data and is used for logins and payments.
  • FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is used to upload and download files to and from a server.
  • POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves emails from a mail server, usually downloading them to one device and removing them from the server.
  • IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) manages emails while keeping them on the server, so they can be read from several devices.
  • SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends emails and passes them between mail servers.

To keep all of these rules manageable, protocols are organised into layers. Each layer deals with just one part of the communication and only has to work with the layers directly above and below it. This means different teams can develop different layers, a layer can be improved or replaced without breaking the others, and faults are easier to track down. A common teaching model splits the whole process into four such layers.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Read the command word carefully: ‘state’ or ‘identify’ wants a short answer for one mark, while ‘describe’ and ‘explain’ want you to add detail and reasons. A very common mistake is mixing up the switch and the router — remember that a switch moves data within a LAN using MAC addresses, while a router moves data between networks using IP addresses. Keep the two kinds of address straight too: a MAC address is permanent, but an IP address can change.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A LAN covers one site and is owned by its organisation, while a WAN covers a large area and connects LANs; the internet is the largest WAN.
  • The DNS turns a web address into an IP address; a switch moves data within a LAN using MAC addresses, and a router moves data between networks using IP addresses.
  • Protocols are agreed sets of rules, such as HTTP for web pages and SMTP for sending email, and they are organised into layers to keep them manageable.

lessons.title: Network Security
lessons.description: How networks are attacked — malware, phishing, DoS — and the defences that stop them.
lessons.content_html:
The Threats Facing a Network

Almost every computer is now connected to a network, and that connection is exactly what attackers try to exploit. Keeping a network secure means understanding two things together: the threats that criminals use, and the defences that block them. Those threats aim at two very different weak spots — the technology itself, and the people who use it.

Key Fact

There are six common forms of attack you should be able to describe: malware, social engineering (such as phishing), brute-force attacks, denial of service attacks, data interception and theft, and SQL injection.

Malware

The word malware is short for ‘malicious software’. Malware is any program written to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a computer system. It usually reaches a machine when a user opens an infected email attachment, downloads a dodgy file, or plugs in an unknown USB stick.

A virus hides inside a file or program and spreads to other files when that program is run, often corrupting data as it goes. A worm is similar but more dangerous on a network, because it can copy itself and spread between computers on its own, without anyone opening a file.

A Trojan is disguised as a useful or harmless program, so the user installs it themselves, only for it to open a back door for the attacker. Ransomware encrypts the user’s files and demands a payment to unlock them, while spyware quietly records what the user does, such as capturing passwords as they are typed.

Social Engineering and Phishing

Social engineering attacks the human user rather than the machine. Instead of breaking through technical defences, the attacker tricks a person into handing over information or access. Because it targets people, staff are often called the ‘weak point’ — even the strongest firewall is useless if an employee simply gives their password away.

The most common example is phishing, where fake emails or text messages pretend to come from a trusted source, such as a bank or the IT department. They usually contain a link to a fake login page designed to steal whatever the victim types in. A sense of urgency, like ‘your account will be closed today’, is a classic warning sign.

Brute-Force Attacks

A brute-force attack is an attempt to crack a password by trying every possible combination in turn until the right one is found. Attackers use software to test thousands of guesses per second, which is why short, common passwords such as ‘123456’ fall almost instantly, while long, unusual passwords take far longer to break.

Denial of Service Attacks

A denial of service attack, or DoS, floods a server with so many requests at once that it becomes overwhelmed and cannot respond to genuine users. The aim is usually not to steal data but to make a website or service unavailable, which can cost a business money and damage its reputation. When the flood comes from many computers at the same time, it is called a distributed denial of service, or DDoS.

Data Interception and Theft

Data interception and theft means capturing data while it travels across a network. Using software called a packet sniffer, an attacker on an unsecured network — such as free public Wi-Fi — can read the packets passing by and pick out useful information like usernames and passwords.

SQL Injection

SQL injection targets the databases that sit behind many websites. If an input box, such as a login field, is not properly protected, an attacker can type in database commands instead of a normal answer.

Databases are searched using a language called SQL. When a website builds its search out of text typed by the user without checking it first, a carefully written entry can change the meaning of that search. This can trick the database into revealing every record, skipping a password check, or even deleting a whole table. The fix is to validate and clean all input before it ever reaches the database.

Key Fact

Many successful attacks rely on human error rather than clever code. People are described as the ‘weak point’ of security because they can be tricked by social engineering, choose weak passwords, or click a malicious link — which is why staff training matters as much as the technology.

Finding and Removing Vulnerabilities

A vulnerability is any weakness an attacker could exploit. One of the best ways to find them is penetration testing, where security experts are paid to attack a system on purpose, in a controlled way, so that weak points can be discovered and fixed before real criminals find them.

Once weaknesses are known, several prevention methods work together to close them:

  • Anti-malware software scans files and memory for malicious programs, then blocks, quarantines or removes anything it finds; it must be updated regularly to recognise new threats.
  • A firewall monitors and filters the traffic passing between a network and the outside world, blocking any connection that breaks its rules.
  • User access levels control what each person is allowed to see or change, so an ordinary user cannot reach the sensitive files that only an administrator should touch.
  • Strong passwords — long, with a mix of letters, numbers and symbols — slow down brute-force attacks, especially when combined with a limit on the number of login attempts.
  • Encryption scrambles data using a key, so that even if it is intercepted it is useless to the attacker without that key.
  • Physical security protects the hardware itself with measures such as locked server rooms, keycard entry and CCTV, stopping anyone from simply walking up to a machine.

No single method is enough on its own, so organisations layer them, an idea known as defence in depth. A firewall might block an attack from the internet, anti-malware catches anything that slips through, encryption protects the data if it is stolen anyway, and access levels limit the damage a single stolen account can do. If one layer fails, the others still stand.

Key Fact

Prevention methods work best in combination: penetration testing finds the weaknesses, then firewalls, anti-malware, user access levels, strong passwords, encryption and physical security each block a different kind of attack.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Watch the command word closely. ‘State’ or ‘identify’ needs only a short answer, ‘describe’ wants you to say what the attack or method actually is, and ‘explain’ wants how or why it works. A very common mistake is muddling threats with prevention methods — if a question asks how to prevent an attack, do not simply name another attack. Whenever you give a prevention method, link it to the specific threat it reduces.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Networks face six main forms of attack: malware, social engineering such as phishing, brute-force attacks, denial of service attacks, data interception and theft, and SQL injection.
  • People are often the weakest point, so tricking a user is frequently easier for an attacker than defeating the technology.
  • Prevention methods — penetration testing, anti-malware, firewalls, user access levels, strong passwords, encryption and physical security — work best when layered together.

lessons.title: Operating Systems & Utility Software
lessons.description: What operating systems do to manage a computer, and how utility software keeps it running.
lessons.content_html:
Behind every app you open and every file you save sits a layer of software you rarely see, called system software. Its job is to control the computer itself and make it usable, so that the programs you actually care about — games, browsers, word processors — have a stable place to run.

The most important piece of system software is the operating system, often shortened to OS. Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS are all operating systems. The OS acts as a bridge between the hardware, the applications and the person using the machine, hiding the complicated details so that everything just works.

The five main jobs of an operating system

The first job is to provide a user interface. On most home computers this is a graphical interface, with windows, icons, menus and a pointer you control with a mouse or touchpad. It gives the user a simple, visual way to run programs and manage files without typing commands. Some systems also offer a command line, where instructions are typed in as text.

The second job is memory management and multitasking. The OS decides how the computer’s memory is shared out, allocating an area of memory to each program that is running and moving data into and out of memory as it is needed. This careful sharing is what allows multitasking, so you can listen to music while writing an essay and keep a browser open at the same time.

The third job is peripheral management. Data has to be transferred between the processor and the many devices attached to a computer, such as printers, keyboards and storage drives, and this flow has to be managed so nothing is lost or muddled. The OS does this using a device driver for each piece of hardware, a small program that translates the OS’s instructions into signals the device understands.

The fourth job is user management. The OS lets a computer have several separate accounts, each with its own settings and files. It controls access rights, deciding what each user is allowed to see and change, which keeps one person’s work private and stops ordinary users from altering important system settings.

The fifth job is file management. The OS organises how data is stored, letting you name files, group them into folders, move and copy them, and save or delete them. It keeps track of where every file is physically stored on the drive so it can be found again instantly.

Key Fact

An operating system carries out five key jobs: providing a user interface, managing memory and multitasking, managing peripherals through drivers, managing users and their access rights, and managing files.

A single processor can really only do one thing at a time, so multitasking is a clever illusion. The operating system gives each running program a tiny slice of processor time in turn, switching between them so quickly that they all appear to run together. To make this work it must allocate each program its own area of memory and transfer data between memory and the processor as each program takes its turn. If a program is not being used at that instant, its data can be moved aside to free memory for the others.

Utility software

Alongside the operating system, computers usually come with utility software. These are small tools that carry out housekeeping tasks — the background jobs that keep a system healthy and secure but that the operating system does not always handle on its own. Three important examples are encryption software, defragmentation and data compression.

Encryption software protects data using encryption. It scrambles the contents of a file into an unreadable form using a key, so that if the file is stolen or intercepted, a thief cannot make sense of it. Only someone with the correct key can turn the data back into its original form. This is vital for confidential information such as passwords, bank details and personal records.

Defragmentation tackles a problem that builds up on hard disk drives over time. As files are saved, deleted and resaved, a single file can end up split into pieces scattered across the drive. Defragmentation software reorganises the drive so the pieces of each file are stored next to each other again. This means the read/write head has less distance to travel, so files load faster.

Data compression software reduces the size of files by encoding them so they use fewer bits. Smaller files take up less storage space and can be sent across a network more quickly, which is why compression is used for photos, music and email attachments. It performs a task the operating system does not do by default, which is exactly why it counts as utility software.

Key Fact

Utility software performs housekeeping tasks the operating system may not. Encryption software scrambles data to keep it secure, defragmentation reorganises scattered files to speed up a drive, and compression shrinks files to save space and transfer time.

On a hard disk drive, data is read by a moving head that travels across spinning platters. When a file is fragmented, its pieces are scattered in different places, so the head has to jump around to collect them all, and each jump takes time. The more fragmented the drive, the more the head has to move, and the slower files load. Defragmentation gathers each file’s pieces back together so the head can read them in one smooth sweep. Solid state drives have no moving parts, so they do not benefit from defragmentation in the same way.

It helps to keep system software and application software separate in your mind. Application software is the programs you use to get a job done, like a spreadsheet or a photo editor. System software — the operating system and utility programs — works quietly in the background to run the machine and keep it in good order so those applications can do their work.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions often ask you to describe a function of the operating system, so learn the five jobs as distinct points rather than blurring them together. When asked to explain how the OS enables multitasking, make the link between allocating memory to each program and switching the processor between them — do not just say ‘it runs many programs’. For utility software, be ready to say why each tool is needed and to name a housekeeping task the operating system does not carry out itself. A frequent slip is to describe defragmentation as deleting files; it reorganises them, it does not remove them.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The operating system is system software that manages the computer and provides a user interface, memory management and multitasking, peripheral management with drivers, user management, and file management.
  • Utility software carries out housekeeping tasks the operating system may not, including encryption to secure data, defragmentation to reorganise scattered files, and compression to shrink file sizes.
  • System software runs and maintains the machine in the background, while application software is what the user runs to complete a task.
